title: Unit 3 rem early
english: It follows, then, that no one is preserved in bodily things or in material possessions, nor even according to nature itself. This is because those who introduce or bring about natures—meaning, those who shape or define what things are by their essence—are the ones who determine preservation. At this point, the soul is directly called “body” by the one who speaks plainly. And Christ, too, in the Gospels, refers to the soul as a body—saying, “The lamp,” he declares, “the eye is the body of it.” He called the lamp the mind, for it is inherently receptive of knowledge. But the body, he says, is the spirited and passionate part of the soul—what some call the irrational part, and others, the emotional or suffering part of the soul. Now, the one who, from the things he makes and teaches, produces good outcomes—first, he gains knowledge of both intelligible and immaterial things in the life to come; and in the age to come, he obtains the kingdom of heaven, securing it for himself and for those who learn from him. He does not merely destroy his own body, but also the soul, along with those who follow him, in the fire of shared destruction. This man—this one who wrongly thrusts hand into hand with violence—is the teacher of evil deeds and false doctrines. But this other one—this one who sows righteousness—is the one who advances in speech concerning virtues and the knowledge of God. To those who sow for their own private gain, and who multiply their holdings, stand opposed those who gather and diminish—because those who sow for themselves are, in fact, those who sow into the spirit and reap life; but those who gather and diminish are those who sow into the flesh and thus gather corruption for themselves. The divine word is like grain: which the Jews, having hidden it away, left behind for the Gentiles. —And this is just like what our Savior says in the Gospels: “No one lights a lamp and then puts it under a bushel basket, but on the lampstand, so that it may give light to all in the house.”

Just as grain serves as nourishment for the body, so divine knowledge sustains the soul. Yet the one who possesses the sustenance of both body and soul but refuses to impart it, instead demanding payment from those who lack it, will be abandoned to the demons. Moreover, he writes a curse upon himself, declaring that he will stand under the judgment of the people of the angels and all the righteous on the day of reckoning, and thus he shall be accursed. The practical cultivation of virtues according to the Spirit is a spiritual craft; but the one who performs what is owed to God seeks out delightful companions—those willing to receive what is due to God—so that, just as he himself engages in exchange, they too may engage in mutual giving. As for those who seek not the good but the evil, they shall be left aside. This tree of life is the one planted in the midst of Paradise, whose fruit Adam was forbidden to touch after his sin, having cast away the seeds of righteousness from which the tree of life grows. Lest you remain silent toward me, says David, and I shall become like those who descend into the pit. A lawless person who falls silent will be forsaken by God—that is, hated and not shown mercy—when he renders the rewards due to those who have received the grace of his incarnate economy, as he says in the Gospels: “And grace for grace.” The wealth of the wicked is evil. But the righteous shall consume them, evidently through wholesome teaching; therefore, even in the age to come, having become fifteen cities, they shall inherit the heavenly inheritance which the impious, having surrendered themselves to impiety, were about to receive—but the righteous shall possess it, as Paul also says in 17:193: “But according to your hardness and unrepentant heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and revelation and of God’s righteous judgment.”

The good one will act as an heir for those who obey him as sons obey their father, and he will adopt them into the heavenly kingdom. For they are invincible, just as weapons produce safety; for nothing evil can stand against wisdom, because it is an unconquerable weapon; only against this are the demons powerless. But to the foolish, both visible things and incorporeal things are entirely opposed. Here he speaks of the bodies as houses; for houses are the dwellings of souls, and they are owed by those who know piety and possess theoretical knowledge. The lawless must learn not only the knowledge of God, but also every commandment of the life-giving ones, so that, having become pure, they may see God with their intellectual eyes. For this is the blessed end, which every rational nature has preserved. And the houses of the righteous are ready to receive all, as the Lord commands. Now he has spoken of the intentions as the divine visions and the dispositions of the virtues, which he set against the ways of the bold-hearted mind. For from the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks, as the Lord said; not to do evil, but to do good, the good man intends in his mind. But the bold-hearted, acting and speaking like a fool, will be filled with scourgings, and with the loss of things, and finally will lose his own soul. Now he has spoken of the rebukes as the commandments; for these reprove us when we sin. And those who hate them,

title: Unit 3 rem mid
english: They die in the shame of their sins, and along with the evil they have invented, they will be dealt with wickedly. However, through those who pass by wickedness, the education of the innocent is recognized as blameless. Quietness is the abstinence from active evil and from seeing evils, which the good practice in stillness. But the eyes of the mind and body of the wicked are constantly contemplating evil throughout all time. Yet the prudent person is not in Hades with the sinners; rather, the ways of life, the thoughts of divine words and deeds—these the prudent person always does and teaches, so that, turning away with their disciples from Hades, they may be saved. Those who do not practice his commandments are his enemies; but they become his friends when they run to the righteous, confessing their wicked deeds. Having been moved by these things, just as those others, they will go on the life-giving ways. For Paul proclaimed: Those who once were enemies were reconciled to God through the death of his Son. Take heed that all enemies, through the righteous, become friends—so that Christ may say to all: No longer do I call you slaves, but friends. Again, there, wisdom is needed to make atonement; either the one who knows the words about punishment is an angel, or the wrath of God is spoken. The wise person in divine works and words, being of one mind with him, will not be startled by him. Nests of wisdom are the churches, or the tents in the heaven; but wisdom is Jesus Christ, the Son of God. Moreover, nests of understanding are better than silver, namely, the practical virtues: justice, knowledge, wisdom, self-control, courage, patience.

Unrebukeable gentleness, freedom from anger, mercy, and faith joined with hope and love: through these, as if climbing the rungs of a ladder, one may enter without hindrance into the dwellings of wisdom, those who wish to ascend and dwell there.
He speaks of discipline as the fear of God, fasting, self-control, vigilance, hymnody, and the discipline that comes upon us in sickness as a testing from God.
He calls rebukes the commandments of God, for these indeed rebuke us when we sin.

He says the ways here are the senses; and the one who guards them preserves his own soul from death toward life, for life is that which sustains all living things, and brings into being from non-existence the Holy Trinity, which causes to be. And the one who loves life, and ever strives to live in it, will refrain from his own mouth the words and works not of God, and will draw near to the knowledge of God.

God is life; and the source of His self-existent, triple-wisdom life is wisdom, knowledge, and the virtues; from this spring those who drink partake of immortality and eternal life; but for those who possess such a spring, there is an understanding of the words of life; yet the discipline of the foolish is folly, and the undisciplined discipline is folly.

He said that knowledge is recognition, because it recognizes all things; and the heart of the wise perceives what comes from its own mouth, both in bodily judgment and in incorporeal matters, and whatever they themselves do, they teach and practice.
The demons, learning words from the devil, attempt against the holy, and imagine themselves trying to separate them from knowledge.

This is her nature, by which she binds them in friendship with the heavenly powers; and the same thing, I believe, Solomon has indicated by this proverb, saying that the twisted man is Satan; but those going about bearing lamps of deceit—namely, the false teachers on his side—he calls evil demons; yet friends, namely, the holy ones, those who through knowledge are touching God and one another. A lawless man, the devil is; and he attempts to tempt the friends of God, and he leads them away to the ways of destruction and not of goodness; but when he has deceived any one of the holy ones, he establishes thoughts for his own eyes, and he considers them twisted, lest perhaps he should save the repentance of him whom he has hunted; and he nibbles with his lips upon his eyes all the evil thoughts, both renunciation and all pleasure of licentiousness; this one is a furnace of all wickedness, and he kindles within it the souls of those who are about to be destroyed; but of this furnace, the divine Spirit quenches the flame, shaking forth wisdom like dew; yet many still of those who are in it, wicked men, are accustomed to imitate their father, the devil. He has said here that the bosoms are the hearts of the unjust; but I think also that everywhere the bosom signifies either the mind, or knowledge; and the wicked indeed the devil embraces in his bosom, but the righteous the Lord. If every one who practices sin is a slave, and every one who departs from wickedness through virtue has held as masters the foolish demons—who also is the house of mysteries of God—

title: Unit 3 rem close
english: It will be, according to the analogy of the feeding, that to each of the brethren is given spiritual knowledge; and so Paul, on the one hand, gave milk to drink to those in Corinth, on the other hand, nourished those in Ephesus with more solid food, speaking concerning height and length and width and depth; and by means of these distinctions he indicates the division of the rational nature, which division encompasses the discourses concerning God's judgment and providence, which discourses are very deeply rooted and lead away from the human condition. Furnaces are the trials; for by means of the trials God elects the warm and the sluggish hearts of the elect. The heretic obeys the tongue of the doctrines of the godless; but those of the Church do not even pay attention. By means of obeying, the voluntary is shown, as if erring into God's wise governance. –This one obeys the tongues of the lawless, he who receives unjust calculations from them and hastens to act according to them; concerning these the righteous is said not to pay attention, to see both the visible and the invisible, that is, not to nourish oneself further within. The faithful, he says, will see the words of this world, which they have figuratively presented as nourishment to the mind; but the unbeliever will not even know the word of any chance thing, on account of the uncleanness of his own soul; for that the wealth of the soul is the knowledge of God, Paul teaches, saying: You have been enriched in everything, in all knowledge and in all wisdom; but if anyone wishes to show that this conception is not this one of mine,

Let those who possess wealth speak of where they acquired their riches—the ones who wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, afflicted, and tormented; how, too, can the unbeliever not possess even a single obol, while many unbelievers, cloaked in great wealth, I mean kings and rulers of this world, abound in riches? Faithful lips declare the virtuous thoughts; but to the foolish, evil thoughts will be acceptable. For what partnership has righteousness with injustice? Unless, perhaps, one who has repented seeks discernment and faith. Through righteousness, we conceal iniquity; through self-control, we conceal intemperance; and again, through love, we conceal hatred; and through freedom from love of money, we conceal greed—yes, the greed quantified as 17.200. We also conceal arrogance through humility, and ferocity through meekness, as we seek spiritual friendship, which signifies holy knowledge; and according to Paul, certain ones among the saints are called fellow citizens, and natives of the heavenly Jerusalem, having been built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets. He says here that the body is the house of the soul; and again, the soul is the house of the mind; and the same mind is called the eye of the soul. But the one who has learned divine knowledge and wisdom, yet has surrendered himself to wickedness, and instead of good words brings forth evil ones, and is unwilling to turn back and be saved—such a person will not see wickedness and depravity depart from the house of his body; rather, they remain firmly entrenched within him, so that complete evil may come upon him, abiding immovable within him on the day of the Lord’s wrath.

The body formed from the earth by the Lord for us, he says, is a house here; and the one that will not be moved, that is, will not depart from its own house, is anger and tribulation, sent forth by men and demons by the Lord, against those who repay good with evil, to the good-doer himself, a human being.

If one who repays evil for evil is lawless, how much more so is one who repays evil for good? Such a one became Israel in the wilderness; to whom Moses says in Deuteronomy: “A crooked and perverse generation, do you repay the Lord thus?” Here he says the beginning is knowledge; and righteousness follows knowledge, for righteousness is begotten from knowledge; but deficiency is ignorance; and strife and battle, every wickedness, precedes ignorance, the wickedness.

Why then do you again accuse the poor? By leading us away from idleness; therefore authority does not come from the laying on of hands; hence, if you wish to walk with boldness, you must be just; and strife and battle precede deficiency, that is, the lack of virtue in those who do wrong.

Such is the one who says the bitter is sweet and the sweet is bitter; and who calls light darkness, and darkness light. Here riches are said to be wisdom and knowledge; but to the foolish, what has the learning of wisdom and knowledge come to? For as a vine cannot grow in thorns, so in folly wisdom cannot bear fruit; for riches are the foolish person’s, the things concerning each particular matter of his.
